ta-l1d47q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 47. Having removed what seemed to take away the efficacy of God's will, Lombard shows that it is always efficaciously fulfilled, then expounds doubts in the authority he used: how something is said to happen against God's will yet not beside it, solved by the various senses of God's will, concluding that God's will, which is himself, is always unconquered. Four articles are announced: whether the will of good pleasure is always fulfilled; whether anything happens beside his will; whether what happens beside his will serves it; and whether what is beside his will can fall under his precept.
claims: God's will, which is himself, is always unconquered.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e118.summary: First argument that God's will is not always fulfilled. A cause open to either alternative is not efficacious, and God's will is, since what he can will he can not will.
claims: God's will is open to either.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e121.summary: Second argument. The effect of an unimpedible cause is necessary, and God's will causes all (Dist. 45), so all would happen necessarily.
claims: Unimpedible cause, necessary effect.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e124.summary: Third argument. A first cause acting through an impedible secondary cause does not produce its effect efficaciously, as the sun's motion causes trees' sprouting through their generative power, which can fail, and God's will is a first cause not excluding fallible secondary causes.
claims: First causes act through fallible secondary causes.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e128.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever God wills now he willed eternally, and eternally he willed to do only what he does, so if he can do only what he wills, he can do only what he does, which is false.
claims: God could only do what he does.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e131.summary: Sed contra. A cause is impeded only by a stronger agent, and nothing is stronger than the divine will.
claims: Nothing can impede God's will.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e134.summary: Second sed contra. Failing to attain what one wills diminishes joy, and God is most happy with most perfect joy.
claims: God's joy is undiminished.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e137.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever God wills by consequent will happens wholly, but not whatever he wills by antecedent will, since he wills this not simply and perfectly but only in some respect, the imperfection being not in the will but in the condition of the thing willed. Will and speculative cognition are opposite here: speculative cognition is perfected by abstraction from singulars, but will and whatever is ordered to work are perfected in the particular, the object of operation. What is simply and perfectly willed is what falls under the will with all the particular conditions surrounding the particular, which belongs to consequent will, regarding works and dispositions by which one is sufficiently ordered to what is fitting and due, and so God is said to will simply, like salvation, and such will cannot be impeded, any more than foreknowledge, to which the thing is subject as actual. What is right and good under some universal condition of the thing does not have the character of willed simply, but only in some respect, as for this man as man it is only good to be saved, his nature being ordered to it, which God wills by antecedent will, by which he is not said to will simply, so such will can go unfulfilled.
claims: God's consequent will is always fulfilled; his antecedent will need not be, being will in some respect.
Will is perfected in the particular with all its conditions, unlike speculative knowledge.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e140.summary: Reply to the first argument. God's will is open to either not by mutability, willing something first and later not, but by liberality, since the act of his will is always in his power, so willing something first and later not willing it are incompossible.
claims: God's freedom is not mutability.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e143.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though God's will is immutable and invincible, not every effect of it is necessary with the absolute necessity a thing has from its proximate cause, but only with conditional necessity, as with foreknowledge (Dist. 38).
claims: God's will imposes only conditional necessity.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e147.summary: Reply to the third argument. Not only the fulfilment of the effect falls under the divine will but the order of all preceding causes under the conditions by which they are determined to the effect without failure, as that this person willing and meriting salvation be saved; the effect with all its causes as unimpeded falls under consequent will.
claims: Consequent will includes the whole order of causes.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God can do nothing that would not be willed by him if it were done, yet many things are in his power that are now neither willed nor good, since they neither are nor ever will be.
claims: God can do what he does not will, which would be willed if done.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e162.summary: First argument that nothing happens beside God's will. 'He who is not with me is against me' (Matt. 12:30), so what is beside God's will is against it, and nothing happens against it, or it would be conquered.
claims: Beside is against.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e168.summary: Second argument. What nothing can happen against or beside is more powerful than what something can happen beside, and God's will is most powerful.
claims: The most powerful admits nothing beside it.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e171.summary: Third argument. Permission has least of the character of will, and nothing happens beside his permission (the text), so much less beside his good pleasure or the other signs.
claims: Nothing escapes permission.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e175.summary: Fourth argument. Augustine says the innocent's office is not only to harm none but to prevent sins, and only sin can happen beside the will of one who wills all goods, so God, most innocent, should prevent rather than permit whatever is beside his will.
claims: The innocent prevent sin.
Things happen beside God's will.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e181.summary: Second sed contra. Many things happen that God does not will to happen (Dist. 46).
claims: God does not will evils.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e184.summary: Thomas's determination. Something happens beside a will either when the will is of the opposite, which is also against the will, or when the will is neither of it nor of its opposite, which is beside but not against it. Regarding consequent good pleasure, things happen beside it but not against it, since all it wills is fulfilled; regarding antecedent will, the opposite of what it wills can happen, so things happen beside and against it. Of the signs, precept, counsel, and prohibition correspond to antecedent will, ordering rational nature to salvation, so things can happen beside and against them. Permission and operation correspond to consequent will differently: operation concerns the effect itself, so as nothing happens against consequent will, nothing happens against operation, only beside it, since the opposite of what God works cannot be, but much happens that he does not work. Permission concerns the cause, subject to consequent will, as able to fail or not, whose effect, failing, belongs to neither will, but to the cause whose capacity permission regards. So what happens beside consequent will does not happen beside permission, and nothing can happen beside or against permission, though the opposite of what is permitted can happen, still according to permission, since permission regards the cause's power to either opposite, so neither is against it and both are according to it.
claims: Things happen beside but not against consequent will; beside and against antecedent will and its signs.
Nothing happens beside or against permission, which regards the cause's power to either opposite.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the first argument. Those not with God are, as far as in them lies, against God as opposing his antecedent will, but do nothing against his consequent will, only beside it, though not beside his permission.
claims: Sinners oppose antecedent will only.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the second argument. That something happens beside God's will is not from its impotence but from the order of his wisdom, which gave things power to either alternative, which is good and willed by consequent will.
claims: God wills things to have power to either alternative.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e194.summary: Reply to the third argument. Permission regards the cause's power to either, so whatever happens does not happen beside it, which is not from nearness to good pleasure, as the objection implied.
claims: Permission encompasses both outcomes.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e197.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The innocent's office is to prevent sins only according to the condition of the sinners: not to bind people lest they sin but to forbid by admonition; so God, preserving human freedom, forbids sins by his laws.
claims: God forbids sin by law, preserving freedom.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e209.summary: First argument that what is against God's will does not serve it. Consequent will is not contrary to antecedent will, and evil beside the divine will is against antecedent will, so it does not serve consequent will.
claims: The two wills are not contrary.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e212.summary: Second argument. Whatever serves the divine will, which always wills good, is ordered to good, and evil in itself is disordered.
claims: Evil is disordered.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e215.summary: Third argument. The good merit by serving God's will and are owed reward, so if the wicked serve his will by sinning, reward is owed for sin, against Rom. 3:8 ('let us do evil that good may come').
claims: Serving God's will merits reward.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e222.summary: Fourth argument. Evil is beside every agent's intention (Dionysius), and what is beside a will's intention does not serve that will, which is of the intended end.
claims: Evil is beside intention.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e225.summary: Sed contra from Gregory in the text.
claims: Even what opposes God serves him.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e228.summary: Second sed contra. God's will is the most powerful cause, and it belongs to power that even what someone strives to do against it yields to its service.
claims: Power turns opposition to service.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e231.summary: Thomas's determination. Everything that happens beside the divine will, even against antecedent will, in a way serves consequent will, which can be taken two ways: as following the conception of the end alone, will of the end in general without determination of means; or as following the conception of means and their condition, will of attaining the end in a determinate way. A builder has two movements of will: one by which he wills to induce the house's form in matter without considering the parts determinately, another by which, considering that this stone suits the foundation, he wills to place it there. Either way, evils serve God's consequent will. As will of the universe's order in general, evil departing from the order of precept falls back into the contrary order (Boethius), of punishment to fault, as a soft, light stone unfit for the foundation is placed at the top of the wall. As will that this foreseen sinner be punished, it serves too, since unless this condition came about in him by sinning, the divine will for his punishment would not be fulfilled, as the stone's heaviness serves the builder's will that it be placed in the foundation.
claims: Evils serve God's consequent will by falling into the order of punishment.
The builder's two wills illustrate will of the end in general and of determinate means.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e234.summary: Reply to the first argument. Antecedent and consequent will are not contrary, since both are of good; that something is against one and not the other but serves it comes from the thing willed, whose conditions are considered differently.
claims: The difference lies in the object's conditions.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e237.summary: Reply to the second argument. As evil is not ordered per se, it does not serve the divine will per se but per accidens, beside the evildoer's intention, since the sinner does not intend by sinning to be punished by God, in which God's will is fulfilled.
claims: Evil serves God per accidens.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the third argument. In good and bad acts there is the act as going out from the agent and as ordered by him to an end. A good act serves God's will in both, since the agent orders it to good by God's good pleasure and God orders it by the consequent good, the reward rendered to merits, and since the human causes this service he merits. A bad act as from the agent is disordered but is ordered by God through the ensuing punishment or a good drawn from it, so the wicked relates only passively to this service, not actively, as the text says God's will is fulfilled concerning him though he does not fulfil it, and so he does not merit, since one merits by acts one causes.
claims: The good serve actively and merit; the wicked serve passively and do not.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e244.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Though evil is beside God's intention, the ordering of evil is intended by God, and the evildoer serves this intention beside his own, doing what is beside God's intention, sin.
claims: God intends the ordering of evil, not evil.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e257.summary: First argument that what is beside God's will, especially sin, cannot fall under precept. A precept indicates God's will, and one who shows himself to will what he does not is a pretender, far from God.
claims: Precept indicates will.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e260.summary: Second argument. Precept corresponds to antecedent will, to which belongs the ordering of nature to good, so nothing against that order can be commanded, and every sin is against the natural law.
claims: Sin is against natural law.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e263.summary: Third argument. No one obeying divine precepts does evil, and some things can only be done badly, joined to an evil end, like envy (Ethics 2).
claims: Some acts are always evil.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e267.summary: Fourth argument. Like things are judged alike, and all sins are alike in being forbidden by divine law, and some, like despairing of God or hating him, can in no way be commanded.
claims: All sins are alike forbidden.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e270.summary: Sed contra. Killing an innocent son is a sin against natural law, yet Abraham was commanded it and praised for obedience; likewise Hos. 1, where the Lord commanded the prophet to take a harlot and have children of harlotry.
claims: Abraham and Hosea received such commands.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e273.summary: Thomas's determination. Precept is a sign of the divine will corresponding to antecedent, not consequent, will, so what is beside consequent will falls under precept, but not what is beside antecedent will. But something in itself beside antecedent will can, with something removed, be of antecedent will, as things evil in themselves, as under a divine precept, receive a character of goodness so that the will should tend to them, which happens with some per se evils and not others. Good in things arises from a twofold order: of all things to the last end, God, and of one thing to another, the first causing the second, since things are ordered to one another to help one another to the last end. So with the goodness from one thing's order to another removed, the goodness from order to the last end can remain, since the first does not depend on the second. Some sins name the disorder of one thing to another, like homicide, fraternal hatred, disobedience to a prelate; if these could keep the goodness from order to the last end, they would be good and the will could tend to them, but this could happen only by divine power, which instituted the order: as only by miraculous divine power can what receives being from the first agent through a secondary cause have being with the secondary cause removed, like an accident without subject in the sacrament of the altar, so only by divine miracle can what is apt to receive goodness from order to the last end through order to some thing have goodness with that order removed. So killing an innocent or resisting a prelate can be good only by divine authority or precept, and no one but God can dispense in such things, as by a miracle. Other sins name disorder from the last end immediately: some sinful acts concern means immediately, and since the form of goodness in means is from the end, the form of malice is departure from the end, and the material element is the act exercised about what is not orderable to the end (the text's examples are fornication and homicide); if another order to the end is conferred on the means, the disorder is removed and the act remains ordered under antecedent will, which only the one who placed that order can do, so what is ordered by divine law is changeable or dispensable only by divine precept, as what a superior has set to be inviolably observed cannot be changed by an inferior. So God made the killing of Isaac, disordered in itself since an innocent son was not ordered to the end by his father killing him, ordered, setting this order: to manifest Abraham's faith and love, as an example to posterity, and to signify Christ's death, and Abraham's will lawfully consented to the killing so ordered by divine authority. Other sins have an act disordered immediately about the end, like sins against God, hating him and despairing of him, and since an act takes its species from its object, these are evil even in their natural species, so their disorder cannot be removed, since ordering them to the end is impossible when by their being they are disordered from it, which would make something ordered and disordered at once; so these never fall under divine precept. Hence God cannot dispense against the precepts of the first table, which order immediately to God, but can against those of the second table, which order to neighbour, though humans cannot.
claims: God can command acts disordered with respect to creatures, conferring on them order to the end, as with Abraham, since the order among creatures serves the order to God.
Acts directly against God, like hatred of God, can never be commanded; God dispenses from the second table, never the first.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e276.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though God did not will by consequent will that Abraham kill his son, he willed by antecedent will that Abraham's will tend to it as already ordered, and the precept expressed such a will, so there was no pretence.
claims: The command expressed antecedent will, without pretence.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e279.summary: Reply to the second argument. Killing an innocent, as under disorder from the end, which comes to it after its species is complete from its proximate object, is against natural law and cannot be done well; but with that disorder removed and another order placed on the object and act, it accords with natural law, which dictates doing whatever is ordered and commanded by God.
claims: Natural law itself commands obeying God's ordering.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e286.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The reasoning is not the same for all sins, as explained.
claims: Sins differ in their relation to the end.

ta-l1d47q1-d1e295.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Whom he justly predestined to punishment' seems against predestination being only of saving goods (Dist. 40), but predestination said absolutely means direction to eternal salvation, while with something added it can be directed to anything, in some respect and less properly. (2) 'Not beside his permission, which he is not' seems against permission being God's operation and his essence, but here permission means its effect, as creation is said passively. (3) Christ commanded the healed not to tell anyone (Matt. 12), willing by consequent will that it not happen as he commanded, yet by antecedent will that people tend not to seek worldly glory, by the example of the man Christ, whose human will sought not his own glory but God's, which the precept expressed.
claims: Predestination to punishment is said only qualifiedly.
Christ's command of silence expressed antecedent will.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 47 divides Lombard's proof that God's will is always efficacious and his solution of doubts by the senses of 'will'. It announces four articles: fulfilment of good pleasure, what happens beside his will, its service to his will, and whether it can be commanded.
claims: God's will is always unconquered.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e110.summary: Article 1 holds that God's consequent will, of the particular with all its conditions, is always fulfilled, while his antecedent will, of the good under a universal condition, is will only in some respect and can go unfulfilled. His freedom is not mutability, his will imposes only conditional necessity, consequent will includes the order of causes, and his power exceeds his will.
claims: Consequent will is always fulfilled; antecedent will need not be.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e154.summary: Article 2 holds that things happen beside but not against God's consequent will, and beside and against his antecedent will and its signs (precept, counsel, prohibition). Nothing happens against operation, and nothing beside or against permission, which regards the cause's power to either opposite. God wills things to have power to either alternative and forbids sin by law, preserving freedom.
claims: Things happen beside consequent will but never against it or beyond permission.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e201.summary: Article 3 holds that evils serve God's consequent will, both as will of the universe's order, since fault falls into the order of punishment, and as will that the foreseen sinner be punished, as a builder places unfit stones where they suit. Evil serves per accidens. The good serve actively and merit, while the wicked serve passively without merit, and God intends the ordering of evil, not evil.
claims: Evils serve God's will passively by falling into the order of punishment.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e249.summary: Article 4 holds that precept expresses antecedent will, so God can command acts disordered with respect to creatures by conferring on them order to the last end, as with Abraham's sacrifice, which manifested faith and signified Christ's death. Acts directly against God, like hatred of God, can never be commanded. So God dispenses from the second table of the Decalogue but never the first, and humans dispense from neither. Abraham's command was without pretence, and natural law itself commands obeying God's ordering.
claims: God can dispense from precepts concerning neighbour, never from those concerning himself.

ta-l1d47q1-Dd1e290.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 47 qualifies 'predestined to punishment', takes 'permission' as its effect, and reads Christ's command of silence as expressing antecedent will.
claims: Predestination to punishment is improper usage.

ta-l1d47q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 47 treats the efficacy of God's will. Article 1 holds that consequent will is always fulfilled, antecedent will not necessarily. Article 2 holds that things happen beside but not against consequent will, and nothing beyond permission. Article 3 holds that evils serve God's will passively, falling into the order of punishment. Article 4 holds that God can command acts disordered toward creatures by ordering them to himself, as with Abraham, dispensing from the second table but never the first.
claims: God's consequent will is always fulfilled, and even evils serve it.
God can dispense from precepts of the second table, never the first.
